title: The Catawba and the northern war parties
summary: For half a century after the Great Peace of 1701, Iroquois and other northern war parties crossed the mountains to strike the Catawba of the Carolina Piedmont, some by way of Kentucky.
bodyMarkdown:
The Catawba never lived in Kentucky, whatever some nineteenth-century writers claimed. For much of the eighteenth century, though, they were the reason northern war parties kept crossing the mountains, and some of those parties walked through the Kentucky country to reach them.

## People of the river

The [Catawba](https://grokipedia.com/page/Catawba_people) are a Siouan-speaking people whose homeland lay along the Catawba River in the Piedmont of the present Carolinas, where Juan Pardo’s Spanish expedition met their ancestors in the 1560s. In the 1700s they were a confederation of towns allied with South Carolina, with a name as hard fighters. In the nineteenth century Henry Rowe Schoolcraft claimed they had once lived in Kentucky before moving south. The ethnologist James Mooney [dismissed the tale](https://grokipedia.com/page/Catawba_people), pointing out that the Spanish had found them on their own river by 1567.

## War turned south

Northern war parties had been striking the southern nations since the 1670s. In August 1701 the [Great Peace of Montreal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Great_Peace_of_Montreal) ended the long wars among the Five Nations Iroquois, New France and the Great Lakes nations. Peace in the north did not end young men’s search for war honors, or the mourning of families who wanted captives to replace their dead. [After 1701 the raids turned south](https://archipel.uqam.ca/10139/) against the Cherokee, the Chickasaw and, above all, the Catawba, whom the French called the Têtes plates, the Flatheads.

French officials, glad to see their allies busy some 800 kilometers from New France and fighting nations tied to England, encouraged the raids until the 1750s.

The Catawba struck back, sometimes chasing raiders north across the Potomac. Colonial governors, who counted both sides as allies, kept trying to stop it. In 1717, during peace talks near Virginia’s Fort Christanna, a [Seneca party attacked unarmed Catawbas](https://blogs.charleston.edu/colonial-carolina/the-committee-of-conference-upon-indian-affairs-report-may-1751/), killing five. A council at Albany in 1721, the Treaty of Lancaster in 1744, and a 1751 voyage by the Catawba leader Haigler to Albany, where he made peace with the Six Nations, each brought a pause. Within two years the attacks had resumed.

## Through the Kentucky country

Some of that traffic crossed Kentucky. The [great warpath network](https://grokipedia.com/page/Great_Indian_Warpath) of the backcountry linked the northern nations with the Catawba and Cherokee towns, and in Kentucky the trail the Shawnee called [Athiamiowee](/stories/athiamiowee-the-warriors-path-through-kentucky/) ran south toward Cumberland Gap. In January 1753 a party of about seventy northern warriors on [an expedition against the southern nations](/stories/odawa-raid-at-eskippakithiki-1753/) fell on Pennsylvania traders in the Kentucky country and on John Finley’s store at Eskippakithiki.

The Shawnee were Catawba enemies too. In 1753 South Carolina jailed six Shawnee warriors who were on their way to attack the Catawba. The most prominent, [Itawachcomequa, called The Pride](https://read.dukeupress.edu/ethnohistory/article-abstract/53/4/657/8615/Shawnee-Origins-of-Their-Seven-Years-War), died in confinement. The Ohio Shawnee answered in 1754 by going to war with the British colonies, a quarrel that ran on and off for sixty years.

## What came after

Smallpox struck the Catawba in 1738 and again in 1759, and by the early 1760s [only about 500 remained](https://grokipedia.com/page/Catawba_people). In 1763 a small Shawnee party killed Haigler near his own town, and in the 1760s South Carolina confirmed a Catawba reservation. The Catawba Nation endured. Its federal recognition came in 1941, was terminated in 1959 and was restored in 1993.

The Catawba story unfolded beyond Kentucky’s borders, so it has no Kentucky map pin.
